On the morning of July 24, 1915, the Eastland was still tied to the dock when it rolled onto its side and killed 844 people.

The Eastland was an excursion steamer. That Saturday it was carrying employees of Western Electric and their families to a company picnic in Michigan City, Indiana. More than 2,500 people came aboard. The gangplank was still down.

The ship had a history. It nearly capsized at its dock in 1904 with about 3,000 people aboard, and it listed severely in Cleveland in 1912. Fast and narrow, the Eastland was top-heavy. The people who ran it knew it had stability problems.

Then a safety reform made those problems worse. After the Titanic sank, a 1915 federal law required more lifeboats. To keep its licensed passenger capacity, the Eastland's operators added lifeboats and rafts high on the upper decks. All that weight sat above the ship's center of gravity.

Shortly after 7 a.m., the Eastland lurched to port and rolled onto its side.

Here is the part that is hard to hold in your head. The ship did not sink. The Chicago River is only about 20 feet deep there, and the hull came to rest about 20 feet from the wharf. Hundreds of people climbed across the exposed side of the ship to the dock and lived.

Hundreds of others were below decks, in the cabins and the dance floor, when the water came in. They had minutes.

844 passengers and crew died, including 590 people under the age of 25. Twenty-two families lost every member.

A grand jury indicted the ship's owners, captain, chief engineer, and federal inspectors. The case was moved to Michigan, where the defendants were found not guilty in February 1916, and the court refused extradition back to Illinois. No criminal trial was ever held in Chicago. No one was convicted.

The Eastland was raised on August 14, 1915. She was sold, and in 1918 she was commissioned as the U.S. Navy's USS Wilmette, serving until 1945 before being scrapped.

The site is a few blocks from the Loop, on a stretch of river where tour boats now run. The water is 20 feet deep. Most days, nobody looks down.

Photographs: National Archives and Records Administration; Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division.

posts.dek: Lakehurst, New Jersey, May 6, 1937. The largest flying machine ever built was seconds from the mooring mast.

On the evening of May 6, 1937, the German passenger airship LZ 129 Hindenburg was approaching the mooring mast at Naval Air Station Lakehurst, New Jersey, to land.

posts.title: The Fire That Was Forgotten
posts.subtitle: The Peshtigo fire, Wisconsin, October 8, 1871
posts.angle: On the same night Chicago burned, a wildfire in Wisconsin killed an estimated 1,500 to 2,500 people, the deadliest in American history, and almost nobody remembers it.
posts.audience: US adults 25-55 who follow history, climate, and forgotten disasters
posts.hook: On the same night Chicago burned, a Wisconsin town was erased. It killed more people.
posts.dek: Peshtigo, Wisconsin, October 8, 1871. The deadliest wildfire in American history happened while the country watched Chicago.
story: On the night of October 8, 1871, the same night the Great Chicago Fire broke out, a firestorm destroyed the lumber town of Peshtigo, Wisconsin. Chicago got the headlines. Peshtigo got a mass grave.
The town was a lumber center. Yards and streets were piled with sawdust, slabs, and slash. A long drought had dried the cutover land. Small fires had been burning in the woods for days.

Then the wind rose into a gale. The separate fires merged into a single wall of flame that moved faster than anyone could run. Survivors described a roaring sound, air that pulled the breath out of them, and a sky that turned orange at noon.
Some people fled to the Peshtigo River and stood in the water for hours while the town burned around them. Others died in the streets, in wells, or in the root cellars where they had hidden.
The fire burned so hot that sand turned to glass in places. The town was gone in about an hour.
The death toll is an estimate. Most accounts say 1,500 to 2,500 people died; some say more. It is still the deadliest wildfire in United States history.
The exact number will never be known. The town was rebuilt, the story faded, and the fire that killed more people than Chicago is usually a footnote in Chicago's story.
posts.payoff: The deadliest wildfire in American history happened the same night as the fire everyone remembers.
posts.cta: Follow for the disasters the textbooks skip.

posts.title: The Dam Nobody Would Fix
posts.subtitle: The Johnstown Flood, Pennsylvania, May 31, 1889
posts.angle: A private club's earthen dam failed above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, and killed 2,209 people. The club's members included some of the richest men in America.
posts.audience: US adults 25-55 interested in history, class, engineering, and accountability
posts.hook: A private club's dam gave way above Johnstown. 2,209 people died.
posts.dek: Johnstown, Pennsylvania, May 31, 1889. The warning was sent. The water was already moving.
story: On May 31, 1889, after days of heavy rain, the South Fork Dam failed above Johnstown, Pennsylvania. The dam held a lake owned by the South Fork Fishing and Hunting Club, a private retreat for Pittsburgh industrialists.

The club had lowered the dam, blocked part of the spillway, and allowed the water to rise. The structure had been patched, not rebuilt. When the rain came, the lake topped the dam and the earth gave way.

A wall of water and debris moved down the Little Conemaugh River. It hit Johnstown with enough force to crush houses, twist railroad tracks, and carry people miles downstream. Fires broke out in the wreckage.
2,209 people died. Thousands more were injured or left homeless. It was, at the time, the deadliest flood in American history.
The club's members included Andrew Carnegie, Henry Clay Frick, and Andrew Mellon. No one was held legally responsible. The courts found that the club owed no duty to the people downstream.

The relief effort was one of the first major tests of the American Red Cross, led by Clara Barton. The disaster also helped push forward the modern debate over who is responsible when private infrastructure fails.
The dam is gone. The club's cottage still stands. The flood is remembered mostly as a story about weather, but the weather was only the trigger.
posts.payoff: The dam was private. The consequences were public.
posts.cta: Follow for the preventable disasters that changed the rules.

posts.title: The Doors That Opened Inward
posts.subtitle: The Iroquois Theatre fire, Chicago, December 30, 1903
posts.angle: A Chicago theater fire killed 602 people in about fifteen minutes. Many of the exits were locked, blocked, or opened inward.
posts.audience: US adults 25-55 interested in history, fire safety, and urban disasters
posts.hook: The fire started on stage. The exits opened inward. 602 people died.
posts.dek: Chicago, December 30, 1903. A matinee at the Iroquois Theatre turned a safety inspection into a warning nobody acted on.
story: On December 30, 1903, a matinee audience packed the Iroquois Theatre in Chicago for the musical Mr. Blue Beard. The theater was new, advertised as fireproof, and filled with about 2,000 people, many of them children.
During the second act, a stage light ignited a muslin curtain. The fire spread into the fly loft and across the painted scenery. The fire curtain that was supposed to seal the stage jammed.

The exits were the real disaster. Some doors were locked. Some were blocked by curtains or scenery. Some opened inward, so a panicked crowd pressing forward held them shut. The stairways to the balconies became choke points.
The fire was out in minutes. The killing took about fifteen minutes. 602 people died, and hundreds more were injured.
The theater had no sprinkler system, no fire alarm, and no fire drill. It had passed inspection. The inspector later testified that he had not checked the exits.
The Iroquois fire led to stricter fire codes in Chicago and across the country. It also changed how theaters were designed, staffed, and inspected.
The building reopened as the Colonial Theatre and was demolished in 1927. The fire is remembered as a case study in how a building can be legal and still be a trap.
posts.payoff: The fire was on stage. The disaster was in the exits.

posts.subtitle: The Monongah mine disaster, West Virginia, December 6, 1907
posts.angle: An explosion in a West Virginia mine killed at least 362 men and boys. It led directly to the creation of the federal Bureau of Mines.

posts.hook: An explosion tore through two West Virginia mines. At least 362 men and boys died.
posts.dek: Monongah, West Virginia, December 6, 1907. The official toll is 362. The community remembers more.
story: At about 10:20 a.m. on December 6, 1907, an explosion tore through mines No. 6 and No. 8 at Monongah, West Virginia. The two mines were connected underground. The blast moved through both.

posts.title: The Blast That Flattened a City
posts.subtitle: The Halifax Explosion, Nova Scotia, December 6, 1917
posts.angle: Two ships collided in Halifax harbour and the munitions cargo detonated, killing about 2,000 people and injuring thousands more.
posts.audience: US adults 25-55 interested in history, maritime disasters, and WWI
posts.hook: Two ships collided in Halifax harbour. Then the munitions cargo detonated.
posts.dek: Halifax, Nova Scotia, December 6, 1917. The largest human-made explosion before the atomic bomb.
story: On the morning of December 6, 1917, the French cargo ship Mont-Blanc was entering Halifax Harbour with a cargo of munitions: TNT, picric acid, benzol, and guncotton. The Norwegian ship Imo was leaving. The two collided in the Narrows.
The collision started a fire. Crowds gathered on the shore and in windows to watch, not knowing what the Mont-Blanc was carrying. At 9:04 a.m., the cargo detonated.
The blast flattened the north end of Halifax. It caused a tsunami in the harbour, snapped trees, twisted steel, and was heard for hundreds of miles. Windows shattered across the city.

About 2,000 people died. Another 9,000 were injured, and 6,000 were left homeless. The Mi'kmaq community of Turtle Grove was destroyed. Many of the dead were children who had been walking to school or watching the fire.
Boston sent a relief train within hours. Halifax has sent Boston a Christmas tree every year since, a tradition that continues today.

The harbour is quiet now. The memorial lists the names. The tree still goes to Boston.

posts.title: The Wave That Came From a Tank
posts.subtitle: The Great Molasses Flood, Boston, January 15, 1919
posts.angle: A storage tank in Boston's North End burst and sent a wall of molasses through the streets, killing 21 people.
posts.audience: US adults 25-55 interested in history, engineering, and strange-but-true stories
posts.hook: A tank of molasses burst in Boston and sent a wave through the streets. 21 people died.
posts.dek: Boston, January 15, 1919. The tank was leaking before it was full. Nobody stopped filling it.
story: On January 15, 1919, a steel tank in Boston's North End burst and released about 2.3 million gallons of molasses. The tank belonged to the Purity Distilling Company and stood fifty feet tall.

The tank had leaked since it was first filled. Neighbors collected molasses from the seams and used it at home. The steel was too thin, the rivets were inadequate, and the tank had never been properly tested.

At about 12:30 p.m., the tank split with a sound that witnesses compared to gunfire. A wave of molasses moved through the streets at an estimated thirty-five miles per hour, pushing buildings off their foundations and twisting the elevated train tracks.
Twenty-one people died. About 150 were injured. Some were trapped in the syrup; others were crushed by debris. The cleanup took months, and the harbor ran brown for weeks.
The company was found liable. The disaster led to stricter building codes and engineering standards for large tanks, and it became a case study in the cost of ignoring obvious warnings.
The site is now a park. The tank is gone. The story is usually told as a curiosity, but it is really a story about a company that knew the tank was failing and kept using it.
posts.payoff: It wasn't a natural disaster. It was a tank that should never have been filled.
posts.cta: Follow for the engineering failures that changed the rules.

posts.title: The Women Who Glowed
posts.subtitle: The Radium Girls, Orange, New Jersey, 1917-1928
posts.angle: Factory workers painted watch dials with radium and were told it was safe. Their bodies became the evidence that changed American labor law.
posts.audience: US adults 25-55 interested in labor history, science, and women's history
posts.hook: They were told the glowing paint was safe. Their bodies became the evidence.
posts.dek: Orange, New Jersey, 1922. The women who painted watch dials with radium were told it was harmless.
story: In the 1910s and 1920s, young women worked at the U.S. Radium Corporation in Orange, New Jersey, painting watch dials with radium paint so the numbers would glow in the dark.
They were told the paint was safe. To keep a fine point on the brush, they shaped it with their lips. Some painted their nails and teeth with the leftover glow for fun.
Radium is a bone-seeker. It lodged in their jaws, bones, and teeth. Workers developed anemia, spontaneous fractures, and necrosis of the jaw. Some lost teeth; some lost parts of their jaws.
The company denied responsibility. Doctors were pressured. The women were told they were hysterical, or that their symptoms were unrelated.
In 1927, Grace Fryer and other workers sued. The case settled in 1928. The women received compensation, but many were already dying.
The Radium Girls case helped establish the field of occupational disease law and pushed forward stronger workplace protections and radiation safety standards.
Their bodies were the evidence. The rules came after. The factories that employed them are gone, but the principle is not: workers should not have to prove they are being poisoned before anyone acts.
posts.payoff: They were told it was safe. Their bodies proved otherwise.

posts.title: The Fire That Changed Burn Care
posts.subtitle: The Cocoanut Grove fire, Boston, November 28, 1942
posts.angle: A Boston nightclub fire killed 492 people. The treatment of its survivors produced the first modern burn protocol.
posts.audience: US adults 25-55 interested in history, medicine, and fire safety
posts.hook: A Boston nightclub went up in flames. 492 people died. Burn care changed forever.
posts.dek: Boston, November 28, 1942. The deadliest nightclub fire in American history.
story: On November 28, 1942, Thanksgiving weekend, more than a thousand people crowded into the Cocoanut Grove, a popular Boston nightclub. The legal capacity was far lower.
The fire started in the basement Melody Lounge, possibly from a match or faulty wiring. It raced through the club's flammable decorations: paper palm trees, cloth drapes, and leather banquettes.
Guests tried to escape through a revolving door and exits that were locked or blocked. Many were crushed in the panic. Others died of burns and smoke inhalation.
492 people died. Another 166 were injured. It is the deadliest nightclub fire in United States history.

The disaster led to fire code reforms across the country, including changes to exit requirements and occupancy limits. It also produced a medical breakthrough: the burn patients at Massachusetts General Hospital became the basis for modern burn treatment and fluid resuscitation.
Owner Barney Welansky was convicted of manslaughter, sentenced to 12 to 15 years, and pardoned by Governor Maurice Tobin after serving four years.
The club is gone. The corner is a memorial. The burn protocol that came out of that night is still taught.
posts.payoff: The fire was fast. The exits were slow.

On November 28, 1942, Thanksgiving weekend, more than a thousand people crowded into the Cocoanut Grove, a popular Boston nightclub. The legal capacity was far lower.

The fire started in the basement Melody Lounge, possibly from a match or faulty wiring. It raced through the club's flammable decorations: paper palm trees, cloth drapes, and leather banquettes.

Guests tried to escape through a revolving door and exits that were locked or blocked. Many were crushed in the panic. Others died of burns and smoke inhalation.

492 people died. Another 166 were injured. It is the deadliest nightclub fire in United States history.

The disaster led to fire code reforms across the country, including changes to exit requirements and occupancy limits. It also produced a medical breakthrough: the burn patients at Massachusetts General Hospital became the basis for modern burn treatment and fluid resuscitation.

Owner Barney Welansky was convicted of manslaughter, sentenced to 12 to 15 years, and pardoned by Governor Maurice Tobin after serving four years.

The club is gone. The corner is a memorial. The burn protocol that came out of that night is still taught.

The tent had been waterproofed with a mixture of paraffin and gasoline. The treatment kept rain out and made the canvas highly flammable.
A fire started near the main entrance. The canvas burned and dripped burning material onto the crowd. The exits were blocked by animal chutes, seating, and panic.
167 people died. More than 700 were injured. Many of the dead were children, and some were never identified.

posts.title: The Ship That Never Left the Dock
posts.angle: A steamship capsized while still secured to its dock, killing 844 people in twenty feet of water, twenty feet from shore.
posts.why: The strongest single story in the slate: an impossible fact in one sentence, real engineering substance, and an abundant free visual archive.
sources: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
posts.imagery: Excellent. Six authentic public-domain frames; renderer complete.
posts.risks: None outstanding. Two common false claims were removed at Gate 2.

posts.title: The Airship That Fell From the Sky
posts.angle: The Hindenburg caught fire while landing at Lakehurst, New Jersey. Thirty-six people died in about thirty-four seconds.
posts.why: An iconic public-domain photograph, a hook that fits in one sentence, and a cause that is still genuinely unresolved.
sources: U.S. National Archives, Hindenburg investigation file
posts.imagery: Excellent. Authentic 1937 photograph of the airship in flames.
posts.risks: Death toll must distinguish 35 on board from 36 total. Cause must stay qualified.

posts.title: The Fire That Was Forgotten
posts.angle: On the same night Chicago burned, a wildfire in Wisconsin killed an estimated 1,500 to 2,500 people, the deadliest in American history, and almost nobody remembers it.
posts.why: The Chicago comparison is a built-in hook and a genuine historical injustice. The purest 'I never knew this' story on the slate.
posts.imagery: Weak. Surviving photographs are scarce and low-resolution. Consider a second visual pass or a text-forward plate.
posts.risks: Death toll is an estimate and ranges widely. Must be presented as an estimate, never a precise figure.

posts.title: The Dam Nobody Would Fix
posts.angle: A private club's earthen dam failed above Johnstown, Pennsylvania, and killed 2,209 people. The club's members included some of the richest men in America.
posts.why: Class, negligence, and documented warnings ignored. The clearest accountability story available, and the imagery is strong.
posts.imagery: Strong. Widely held period photographs, public domain.
posts.risks: The club's responsibility is documented but the legal outcome needs precision. Avoid a simple morality play.

posts.title: The Doors That Opened Inward
posts.angle: A Chicago theater fire killed 602 people in about fifteen minutes. Many of the exits were locked, blocked, or opened inward.
posts.why: A direct safety-failure story with a physical mechanism a reader can picture, and Chicago continuity with Post 001.
sources: National Fire Protection Association historical records
posts.imagery: Strong. Period photographs, postcards, and architectural images.
posts.risks: Graphic subject. No imagery of victims. Verify each specific exit failure before naming it.

posts.title: The Worst Mining Disaster in American History
posts.angle: An explosion in a West Virginia mine killed at least 362 men and boys. It led directly to the creation of the federal Bureau of Mines.
posts.why: Labor history with a concrete policy consequence, and a death toll that is still argued over.
posts.imagery: Moderate. Period photographs exist but are low-resolution or graphic. Cover is a disclosed reconstruction.
posts.risks: Death toll varies from 362 to over 500. Child labor is central and needs care. Dignity review required.

posts.title: The Blast That Flattened a City
posts.angle: Two ships collided in Halifax harbour and the munitions cargo detonated, killing about 2,000 people and injuring thousands more.
posts.why: Enormous scale, a clear chain of events, a strong human-response beat, and a warm US-Canada payoff.
posts.imagery: Strong. Period photographs are public domain in Canada and the US.
posts.risks: Non-US story; needs a clear reason for a US audience. Verify the death toll and the Turtle Grove story.

posts.title: The Wave That Came From a Tank
posts.angle: A storage tank in Boston's North End burst and sent a wall of molasses through the streets, killing 21 people.
posts.why: The hook is irresistible and the underlying failure, a tank built too thin and never properly tested, is genuinely instructive.
posts.risks: Tone is the whole risk. It reads as trivia if handled lightly. Verify the claimed wave speed and the toll.

posts.title: The Women Who Glowed
posts.angle: Factory workers painted watch dials with radium and were told it was safe. Their bodies became the evidence that changed American labor law.
posts.why: Human, scientific, and legally consequential. It broadens the season beyond disasters into science and labor.
sources: Illinois and New Jersey state archives
posts.imagery: Moderate. The factory photograph is authentic but soft. Portraits are limited and rights vary.
posts.risks: Portrait rights need per-item verification. Avoid lurid medical detail. Verify names, dates, and legal outcomes.

caption_formula: Hook in the first 125 characters, before the 'more' cut.
Context: place, date, and the specific situation.
Turn: the detail that makes the story surprising.
Evidence: numbers, names, and the mechanism.
Payoff: the sentence the reader remembers.
CTA: one clear ask, never engagement bait.
Credit: photographer or archive, plus AI disclosure if relevant.

hashtag_strategy.instagram: Use 5-6 tags: one broad (#History), two topical (#MaritimeHistory), one local (#ChicagoHistory), one specific (#EastlandDisaster). Rotate the broad tag. Never use banned or irrelevant tags.
hashtag_strategy.facebook: Use 3-4 tags. Facebook rewards fewer. Put them at the end, after the credit. Do not use hashtags as a sentence.
hashtag_strategy.rule: Specific beats popular. A tag with 20k posts that describes the story is worth more than a tag with 20M posts that describes nothing.

seo_checklist: One focus keyword per post; it appears in the title, meta description, slug, first 100 words, and image alt.
SEO title 50-60 characters; meta description 140-160 characters.
Slug is short, lowercase, hyphenated, and stable.
Canonical URL is absolute and matches the slug.
Open Graph title and description are written separately from the SEO title.
Every image has descriptive alt text, not a keyword dump.
Internal links point to two related stories.
Article schema includes headline, datePublished, author, and image.
No duplicate meta descriptions across posts.
Re-check character counts after every edit.

platform_rules.instagram: 4:5, 1080x1350, JPEG q92, up to 20 carousel images. Caption max 2,200 characters. First 125 characters are the hook. Alt text per image. 5-6 hashtags.
platform_rules.facebook: 4:5 or 1:1, 1080x1350. Caption can be long, but the feed cuts around 125-250 characters. 3-4 hashtags. Alt text per image. Put the credit before the hashtags.

measurement: Reach and impressions at 1 hour, 24 hours, 72 hours, and 7 days.
Saves and shares per reach; these are the strongest quality signals.
Profile visits and follows per post.
Comments that ask a real question, not just emoji.
Link clicks if a link is used.
Watch time and completion rate for Reels adaptations.
Unfollows and negative feedback; investigate any spike.
engagement: Reply to every substantive comment within 60 minutes of publishing.
Pin a comment with the source list and any correction.
Ask one honest question at the end; never use rage bait.
Correct errors publicly and link the correction in the first comment.
Do not argue with commenters; move the dispute to a source.
Save the best questions for the next post in the cluster.
playbook.ai_policy: Authentic archival imagery first. Use an editorial reconstruction only when no usable, rights-clear image exists. Label it on the image and in the caption. Never present an AI image as documentary evidence.
